sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. Research on the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. Afrika und Übersee 93: 3-44. DOI 10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.209.
sources.note: Silent (zero occurrences of stress/accent/tone in the whole article). p. 22: 'Material on the Gyong [Kagoma] language appears in Gerhardt (1983a) and Hagen (1988).' Bibliography adds Gerhardt 1973/4 'Proto-Benue-Congo und Kagoma' (AuU 57: 81-93) and Adwiraah & Hagen 1983.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. Verbal pluralization strategies in Plateau. Afrika und Übersee 93. DOI 10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.211.
sources.note: Silent; only a handful of Gyong verb pairs (fɛt/fɛza 'kill', ze/zena 'go') in comparative tables.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2018. Nominal affixes and number marking in the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. In John R. Watters (ed.), East Benue-Congo: Nouns, pronouns, and verbs, 107-172. Berlin: Language Science Press. Section 2.3.6 Gyongic, pp. 132-133.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Second-hand from Hagen 1988: 'Gyong marks plurals with prefix alternation, palatalisation alternation and tone'; reproduces tone-marked (H/L) Gyong forms from Hagen (kìdzí 'blood', kìpɛ̀ndɛ̀m kìlúm 'large farm'); 'Stem-tone changes multiply the possible number-marking strategies.' No word 'stress' in the Plateau chapter.

sources.citation: Ibrahim, Musa Rhoda. 2010. A contrastive analysis of the noun phrase in Gyong and English. MA thesis (Dept. of English), Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. 140 pp. Kubanni handle 123456789/5205.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Silent on stress. Whole text searched (stress/accent/pitch/prosody): every 'stress' hit concerns English. Only prosodic remark on Gyong: noun class 5 = 'Nouns that pluralize by switch in tone (from H to L, e.t.c)' (thesis pp. 22-27), i.e. tone is lexically/grammatically contrastive; no statement about word stress.

sources.citation: WALS Online, language Kagoma (wals_code_kgm), source Hagen 1988; CLDF cldf-datasets/wals).
sources.note: Kagoma has exactly one WALS datapoint (72A Imperative-Hortative Systems, Hagen 1988: 149, 170); no stress (14A-17A) or tone (13A) coding, so no second-hand stress statement exists there.

sources.citation: Hagen, Eva. 1981. Das Kagoma: Untersuchungen zu einer zentralnigerianischen Klassensprache. Magisterschrift, Universität Hamburg. 146 Bl.

sources.note: Earlier and (per Glottolog) longer sketch by the same author; may carry the phonological groundwork (tone and accent) that the 1988 monograph condenses. Unpublished; Hamburg SUB copy is marked 'nicht für den Austausch'.

sources.citation: Hagen, Eva. 1988. Die Gong: monographische Studie zu Kultur und Sprache der Gong (Kagoma), Zentralnigeria. Hamburg: Krämer. 181 pp. (Diss. Hamburg 1987/88).
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: The only published monographic description of the language (Glottolog MED; the source of all Gyong data in Blench 2018 and WALS). A Hamburg Africanist dissertation of this era normally opens with a Lautlehre/phonology chapter including Ton and Akzent; the only realistic home of a stress statement.

sources.citation: Adwiraah, Eleonore & Eva Hagen. 1983. Nominalklassensystem des Gworok und des Gyong. In R. Voßen & U. Claudi (eds.), Sprache, Geschichte und Kultur in Afrika, 15-33. Hamburg: Buske.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Short Gyong noun-class paper by Hagen; low chance of a stress statement but it is the only other first-hand Gyong publication.

sources.citation: Gerhardt, Ludwig. 1983. Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Sprachen des nigerianischen Plateaus. Glückstadt: J.J. Augustin. 246 pp.

sources.note: Comparative-descriptive monograph that Blench 2020 names (with Hagen 1988) as one of the two sources of material on Gyong; Google Books snippets show it treats pitch/tone systems of the Hyam (Jaba) subgroup, so it may characterise Kagoma prosody as well.
